opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I've always thought about it is that pretraining gives you an enormous amount of knowledge, but not necessarily the right *behavior*. When you train a model to predict the next token on internet-scale text, it learns to imitate the full distribution of what people write: the brilliant explanations, but also the confused ones, the half-finished arguments, the wrong answers stated confidently. The objective doesn't distinguish between "what's likely to come next" and "what's actually good or correct."

So there's a gap between imitation and intent. If you ask a pretrained model a hard question, it might give you a plausible-sounding continuation rather than the answer you actually want. Supervised fine-tuning helps close some of that gap, because you show it examples of good responses. But you're still limited by the demonstrations you can collect, and in many domains it's much easier for a person, or a checker, to recognize a good answer than to write one.

That asymmetry is where reinforcement learning becomes really powerful. Instead of telling the model exactly what to say, you give it a signal about outcomes: was this helpful, was this proof correct, did this code pass the tests. Then the model can explore and discover strategies that weren't explicitly in the training data. It can learn to check its work, back up when it's going down a bad path, or spend more effort on harder problems.

Another piece is that pretraining is essentially passive. The model never sees the consequences of its own outputs. RL closes that loop: the model generates something, gets feedback, and adjusts. That's much closer to how we think about learning in people, where you improve by acting and seeing what happens, not just by reading.

So pretraining builds the foundation, the knowledge and the representations, and RL is how you shape that into reliable, goal-directed behavior. And increasingly, I think it's how you get capabilities, especially in reasoning, that go beyond what imitation alone can give you.

r001.rationale: The response says RL can help a model check its work and back up from a bad path, but it does not state that pretraining alone failed to teach the model to revise its own writing.

r002.rationale: It says next-token training does not distinguish likely continuations from good or correct answers, but does not say the model cannot distinguish good parts from bad parts of its own writing.

r003.rationale: The response describes feedback on outcomes such as helpfulness, proof correctness, and code tests; it does not identify RL as recognizing when generated text fails to resemble intended language.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Thanks for having me. The short answer is that pretraining gives you a model that's very good at predicting what text looks like, but that's not the same as a model that's good at doing what you actually want. When you train on the whole internet, the objective is next-token prediction, and the model learns to imitate the distribution of human writing, including all the mediocre, wrong, or unhelpful parts. It doesn't have any notion of "this answer is better than that one." It just knows "this is plausible."

So the problem we kept running into was that the capability was clearly in there. You could prompt the model carefully, show it a few examples, and it would do remarkable things. But getting that behavior reliably, without heavy prompting, was hard. Supervised fine-tuning helps, but it has a ceiling, because you're limited by what your human labelers can write, and honestly, for a lot of tasks it's much easier for a person to judge which of two responses is better than to write the ideal response from scratch.

That's really the insight behind reinforcement learning here. You shift from imitating demonstrations to optimizing against preferences or outcomes. The model proposes something, you get a signal about whether it was good, and you push the model toward more of that. That lets it go beyond its training data in a sense. It can discover behaviors that no single human example showed it, as long as you can recognize them as good.

And once you have that loop, it generalizes in interesting ways. For things like math or code, you don't even need human preferences; you have a verifiable answer, and the model can learn from thousands of its own attempts. That's where a lot of the recent gains in reasoning have come from. Pretraining builds the raw knowledge, and reinforcement learning is how you turn that into judgment.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining does not ensure desired behavior, but it does not mention revising the model’s own writing.

r002.rationale: It says the model lacks a notion of which answer is better, but does not state that pretraining cannot distinguish good parts of its own writing from bad parts.

r003.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning as optimizing preferences or outcomes, but not as detecting when generated text differs from the intended language.

astra-6.text:
Pretraining teaches a model to predict what comes next in text, but that isn’t quite the same as teaching it to be a good assistant. A plausible continuation might be helpful, or it might be misleading, evasive, or simply irrelevant to what you wanted.

The motivation for reinforcement learning was to give the model a signal about the quality of the whole response. Instead of only asking, “Did you predict the next word correctly?” we could ask, “Did this answer actually help the user?” Human feedback gives us a way to express those preferences, and reinforcement learning lets us optimize toward them.

So pretraining gives you a broad foundation of capabilities. The work afterward is about getting the model to use those capabilities in ways that better match what people are asking for.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining alone may not produce a good assistant, but does not say it fails to teach models to revise their own writing.

r002.rationale: It discusses evaluating the quality of a whole response, not distinguishing good parts of the model’s writing from bad parts.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning optimizes responses toward human preferences, but does not say it helps models recognize when generated text differs from intended language.

sol-6.1.text:
Pretraining teaches a model to predict the next word, but that’s not quite the same as teaching it to be helpful. If you ask a question, there are lots of plausible continuations: it could answer, repeat the question, or continue a discussion about something else. The pretraining objective doesn’t explicitly distinguish which of those you actually wanted.

The idea with reinforcement learning was to give the model a signal about the quality of the whole response. You could generate different answers, have people indicate which they preferred, and use that feedback to make useful answers more likely. So we weren’t trying to replace pretraining. We wanted to take the capabilities it had learned and steer them toward what people were asking it to do.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining does not explicitly teach helpfulness, but it does not say pretraining is insufficient for revising the model’s own writing.

r002.rationale: It discusses feedback on the quality of a whole response, not distinguishing good parts of the model’s writing from bad parts.

r003.rationale: It describes using preference feedback to make useful answers more likely, but does not identify recognizing a mismatch with intended language as reinforcement learning’s role.
